# Hackathon Requirements — Banking / NBFC Risk & Compliance Copilot

## 1. Problem Statement

Banking and NBFC teams manage:

- **Real-time fraud** detection
- **Liquidity risk** and **credit risk**
- **Regulatory reporting** — AML, Basel, and local regulations

These workflows are **largely manual today**.

## 2. Core Objective

Build a **copilot** that:

- Surfaces **risk and fraud signals**
- Produces **audit-ready regulatory outputs**
- Driven entirely from **natural language questions**

## 3. Functional Requirements

| # | Requirement |
|---|---|
| FR-1 | Combine **structured** transaction and account data with **unstructured** policy and filing text |
| FR-2 | Let a **business or compliance user** ask questions and receive **governed, explainable, evidence-backed** answers |
| FR-3 | Cover the full flow: **signal → evidence → documented finding or report** |

### FR-1 — Data Fusion
- Structured: transactions, accounts
- Unstructured: policy documents, regulatory filings
- Both must be queryable together in a single answer path

### FR-2 — Answer Quality Bar
- **Governed** — access-controlled, policy-respecting
- **Explainable** — the user can see *why* an answer was given
- **Evidence-backed** — every claim traceable to source data or source document

### FR-3 — End-to-End Flow
1. **Signal** — detect/surface a risk or fraud indicator
2. **Evidence** — assemble the supporting structured records and document excerpts
3. **Finding / Report** — emit a documented, audit-ready output

## 4. Judging Criteria

- **Real World Relevance**
- **Technical Execution**
- **Solution Completeness**

## 5. Mandatory CoCo Lifecycle Coverage

All solutions **must use CoCo (CLI or Desktop app) across the full lifecycle**. Judges will look for evidence at **every** stage.

| Phase | What must be done in CoCo | Evidence to show |
|---|---|---|
| **Planning** | Explore the data, frame the problem, draft the solution design, outline the data model, ontology, and workflow — **before any build begins** | Design docs / plans produced via CoCo, data exploration transcripts |
| **Development** | Build pipelines, semantic views, models, agents, and application code — **iterating in the CLI or Desktop app rather than by hand** | Session history showing CoCo-driven builds and iteration |
| **Execution** | Run and orchestrate the **complete end-to-end** solution through CoCo, including **scheduled or automated runs** where the scenario calls for it | Live/recorded end-to-end run, automation definitions |
| **Testing & Validation** | Validate outputs, test accuracy, handle **errors and edge cases**, confirm correct behaviour **before the demo** | Validation runs, accuracy checks, edge-case handling |

## 6. Recommended CoCo Tasks to Demonstrate

| # | Task | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| RT-1 | **Synthetic data generation** | Generate realistic, **referentially consistent** synthetic or de-identified datasets so **no production data is ever needed** and privacy is respected from the start |
| RT-2 | **Data pipeline creation** | Build and orchestrate ingestion + transformation pipelines (dynamic tables, tasks, streams) through CoCo, including **incremental and near-real-time** flows |
| RT-3 | **Semantic model & ontology authoring** | Infer and generate semantic views, **verified queries**, and the ontology from a schema — then **validate them against natural language questions** |
| RT-4 | **Streamlit report / app generation** | Scaffold and run a Streamlit report or app through CoCo to present insights and let users **take action inside the solution** |
| RT-5 | **Connecting additional sources via MCP** | Wire in external systems and tools via MCP (e.g. Jira, Slack, Google Drive, other MCP servers) so the agent can **read from and act across** those tools |
| RT-6 | **Document & unstructured processing** | Parse, extract, and enrich documents with CoCo and **combine them with structured data** for richer answers |

## 7. Ingenuity / Bonus Points

| # | Capability | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| B-1 | **Reusable & shareable skills** ⭐ | Publish custom skills or agent skills other teams could reuse. Clearly documented, reusable skills are the **headline bonus** |
| B-2 | **MCP connectors to external tools** | Extend the solution to more sources/tools via MCP, turning read-only analysis into **cross-tool action** |
| B-3 | **Automations & scheduled runs** | CoCo automations — scheduled tasks (CLI/Desktop) or asynchronous runs — so the solution operates **unattended on a schedule** |
| B-4 | **Custom tools & function calling** | Register custom tools/functions the agent can call to **take real actions**, not only return text |
| B-5 | **Multi-agent orchestration** | Coordinate several agents or skills into one workflow with **clear handoffs and shared context** |
| B-6 | **Working across surfaces** | Same solution across CoCo **CLI**, **Desktop app**, and **Snowsight Cloud Agents** — and surfaced through the **Slackbot** where useful |
| B-7 | **Guardrails & graceful fallback** | Validation, error handling, **confidence checks**, and governed behaviour so the agent **fails safely and stays trustworthy** |

- [ ] Copilot surfaces risk **and** fraud signals
- [ ] Copilot produces **audit-ready** regulatory outputs
- [ ] Input is **natural language questions**

Migrate from streams and tasks to dynamic tables
Dynamic tables replace imperative pipeline code (INSERT, MERGE, stored procedure calls) with a declarative model: you write a SELECT that describes the result you want, and Snowflake keeps it fresh.
This page covers how to convert streams-and-tasks pipelines to dynamic tables one task at a time.

Choose a migration strategy
Dynamic tables support two operational models. Choose the one that fits your team’s workflow.
Self-refreshing dynamic tables (Snowflake manages timing)
Set a TARGET_LAG value and Snowflake handles the refresh schedule. This is the simplest model and is suited for new pipelines or teams that want to reduce operational overhead.
Copy codeCREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE dt_orders
    TARGET_LAG = '10 minutes'
    WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
AS
    SELECT ...
    FROM raw_orders;

Best for:

New pipelines where you don’t already have orchestration in place.
Teams that want Snowflake to manage refresh timing and dependency ordering.
Pipelines where a freshness goal (such as “no more than 10 minutes stale”) is the correct requirement.


Orchestrator-managed dynamic tables (SCHEDULER = DISABLE)
If you already run an orchestrator (dbt, Airflow, or even tasks), create dynamic tables with SCHEDULER = DISABLE. Snowflake does not schedule refreshes automatically. You trigger each refresh manually or from your orchestrator. Refreshes do not cascade upstream or downstream.
Copy code-- Create the dynamic table with scheduling disabled.
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE dt_orders
    WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
    SCHEDULER = DISABLE
AS
    SELECT ...
    FROM raw_orders;

-- Trigger a refresh manually or from your orchestrator.
ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE dt_orders REFRESH;

Key behaviors:

You can’t set TARGET_LAG when using SCHEDULER = DISABLE.
Refreshes with SCHEDULER = DISABLE do not cascade upstream or downstream. Each dynamic table refreshes independently.
Your orchestrator controls the order, timing, and error handling.

Teams that want to keep their existing orchestrator while adopting declarative definitions.
Pipelines that require explicit control over refresh order or conditional refresh logic.

The following patterns convert cleanly from streams and tasks to dynamic tables.

Append-only ingestion
This is the simplest migration. A stream and task that inserts new rows into a target table becomes a single
dynamic table.
Set up the base table and sample data first. This example uses the same raw_orders table from

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE clean_orders (

    customer_id    INT,
    order_date     TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
    product_name   VARCHAR,
    quantity       INT,
    unit_price     DECIMAL(10,2),
    line_total     DECIMAL(12,2),
    order_status   VARCHAR

    WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
    SCHEDULE = '10 MINUTE'
    WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('raw_orders_stream')
AS

    SELECT
        order_id,
        customer_id,
        order_date,
        TRIM(UPPER(product_name)) AS product_name,
        quantity,
        unit_price,
        quantity * unit_price AS line_total,
        order_status

    WAREHOUSE = transform_wh

accurately represents the current state of the base table matching the WHERE filter. If the base table only

Decision guide for dynamic tables
Use this guide to choose the right approach for your data pipeline: dynamic tables, streams and tasks,
or materialized views.


Decision table
ScenarioDynamic tablesStreams and tasksMaterialized viewsSQL-based pipeline with joins or aggregationsPreferredPossibleNo (single table only)Multi-step declarative pipeline (bronze/silver/gold)PreferredPossibleNoIncremental processing of changed dataPreferred (declarative)Preferred (procedural)NoSingle-table query accelerationPossiblePossiblePreferredProcedural logic (stored procedures, IF/ELSE, loops)NoPreferredNoMERGE or complex upsert patternsNoPreferredNoExternal function calls or API integrationsNoPreferredNoAlways-current data with no lagNo (minimum TARGET_LAG setting is 1 minute)Possible (tasks run on a schedule; not zero-lag)PreferredTransparent query acceleration (optimizer rewrites queries to use the precomputed result)NoNoPreferredCustom scheduling or strict orchestration controlPossible (manual trigger only; no CRON or cascade)PreferredNoPipeline using UDFs, UDTFs, or SnowparkPossible (scalar UDFs and UDTFs with explicit column lists; Snowpark not supported)PreferredNoExpandShow lessSee more
If you need X, use Y
Use the following guidance to match your requirements to the right approach.
If you need a declarative SQL pipeline, use dynamic tables
Dynamic tables let you define the result you want as a SELECT statement. Snowflake handles refresh timing,
dependency ordering, and incremental processing. You don’t need to write procedural code, manage streams, or
build a pipeline of tasks.
This is the recommended approach for new multi-table SQL pipelines in Snowflake, especially
pipelines with joins, aggregations, or window functions.
If you need procedural logic or custom orchestration, use streams and tasks
Streams and tasks give you full control over the pipeline logic. Use them when your pipeline needs
stored procedures, MERGE operations, external function calls, custom retry logic, or explicit scheduling
with CRON expressions. For more information, see Introduction to streams and
Introduction to tasks.
If you need single-table query acceleration, use materialized views
Materialized views accelerate repeated queries against a single base table. The query optimizer automatically
rewrites queries to use the materialized view, and the data is always current. Use materialized views when
your goal is read performance, not building a data pipeline. For more information, see
Working with Materialized Views.
Example: streams and tasks vs. dynamic tables
The following side-by-side comparison shows how the same definition (extracting names from raw JSON data)
looks with each approach. The dynamic table version replaces the stream, task, and MERGE logic with a single
SELECT statement.
Streams and tasks approach
Create a landing table.
Create a stream on the landing table.
Create a target table.
Create a task with MERGE logic to process stream records.
Resume the task.

Dynamic table approach
Create a landing table.
Create a dynamic table with the SELECT that defines the result.

Streams and tasksDynamic tablesCopy code-- Create a landing table to store
-- raw JSON data.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw
  (var VARIANT);

-- Create a stream to capture inserts
-- to the landing table.
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM rawstream1
  ON TABLE raw;

-- Create a table that stores the
-- names of office visitors from the
-- raw data.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE names
  (id INT,
   first_name STRING,
   last_name STRING);

-- Create a task that inserts new name
-- records from the rawstream1 stream
-- into the names table.
-- Run the task every minute when
-- the stream contains records.
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK raw_to_names
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  SCHEDULE = '1 minute'
  WHEN
    SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('rawstream1')
  AS
    MERGE INTO names n
      USING (
        SELECT var:id id, var:fname fname,
               var:lname lname,
               metadata$action,
               metadata$isupdate
          FROM rawstream1
      ) r1 ON n.id = TO_NUMBER(r1.id)
      WHEN MATCHED
        AND metadata$action = 'DELETE'
        AND NOT metadata$isupdate THEN
          DELETE
      WHEN MATCHED
        AND metadata$action = 'INSERT' THEN
        UPDATE SET n.first_name = r1.fname,
                   n.last_name = r1.lname
      WHEN NOT MATCHED
        AND metadata$action = 'INSERT' THEN
        INSERT (id, first_name, last_name)
          VALUES (r1.id, r1.fname, r1.lname);

-- Start the task.
ALTER TASK raw_to_names RESUME;
Copy code-- Create a landing table to store
-- raw JSON data.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw
  (var VARIANT);

-- Create a dynamic table containing
-- the names of office visitors from
-- the raw data.
-- Keep the data within 1 minute of
-- the base table.
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE dt_visitors
  TARGET_LAG = '1 minute'
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL
  AS
    SELECT
      var:id::int id,
      var:fname::string first_name,
      var:lname::string last_name
    FROM raw;
ExpandShow lessSee more
The dynamic table approach replaces four objects and MERGE logic with a single SELECT definition.
When NOT to use dynamic tables
Don’t use dynamic tables when your pipeline has any of the following requirements. Use streams and tasks
or materialized views instead, as noted.
You need DML on the output table
Dynamic tables are read-only. You can’t run INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE against them. If your pipeline
requires direct modifications to the output (for example, GDPR right-to-erasure requests), use streams
and tasks with a standard table.
You need stored procedures or external functions
The dynamic table definition can’t call stored procedures, external functions, or tasks. If your pipeline
requires procedural logic, conditional branching, or external API calls, use streams and tasks.
You need sub-minute data freshness
The minimum target lag for a dynamic table is 1 minute. If you need always-current data with no lag,
use materialized views. If you need sub-minute freshness with custom logic, use streams and tasks.
You need MERGE or complex upsert patterns
Dynamic tables use a declarative model and don’t support MERGE statements. If your pipeline relies
on upsert logic with compound keys, use streams and tasks.
You need surrogate key generation
Dynamic tables don’t support sequence functions (SEQ1, SEQ2) or UUID_STRING in incremental
refresh mode. RANDOM() is not supported in incremental refresh mode. If you use AUTO, it resolves to FULL when the definition includes RANDOM(). If your pipeline generates surrogate keys with these functions, use streams and tasks.
Timestamp functions like CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are supported in WHERE/HAVING/QUALIFY clauses. See supported queries for the full matrix.
You need schema evolution without reinitialization
Changing the definition of a dynamic table (for example, adding columns) triggers reinitialization (Snowflake reprocesses the entire table). If your pipeline requires frequent schema changes without reprocessing all data, use streams
and tasks with ALTER TABLE.
You need SCD Type 2 history tracking
Dynamic tables represent the current state of the data, not a historical record. If your pipeline
needs to track changes over time (slowly changing dimensions Type 2), use streams and tasks.
Your definition is a simple single-table query
If you only need to accelerate a query against a single base table without joins, a materialized view
is more efficient. The query optimizer automatically rewrites queries to use the materialized view, which
doesn’t happen with dynamic tables.

Key limitations
A single account can hold a maximum of 50,000 dynamic tables.
You can’t run DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE) on a dynamic table.
You can’t create a temporary dynamic table.
Dynamic tables don’t support sources that include directory tables, external tables, streams, or materialized views.
Frozen region predicates have restrictions on supported expressions. For details, see Frozen regions and backfill.
For the full list of limitations, see CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE.

For queries supported in dynamic table definitions, see Supported queries for dynamic tables.
If you chose streams and tasks, see Introduction to streams and Introduction to tasks.
If you chose materialized views, see Working with Materialized Views.

3. Use streams on dynamic tables

   Markdown URL (preferred for web_fetch, falls back to URL above on 404): https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/dynamic-tables/streams-on-dts.md

Use streams on dynamic tables
A stream on a dynamic table captures row-level inserts, updates, and
deletes. Each read returns the net changes since the previous read. This lets you bridge a dynamic table pipeline into targets that
dynamic tables can’t reach on their own, such as stored procedures, external API calls, or
conditional logic in a task.
This example assumes you have an existing dynamic table named dt_orders that uses an incremental
refresh. See Create a dynamic table for setup guidance.
ImportantUse the ON DYNAMIC TABLE syntax when creating the stream. ON TABLE doesn’t work with dynamic
tables and returns an error. See Common error for an
example.
Copy codeCREATE OR REPLACE STREAM dt_orders_stream ON DYNAMIC TABLE dt_orders;


Supported stream types
Streams on dynamic tables support only the standard (delta) type. The standard stream captures
inserts, updates, and deletes as net changes since the stream was last read.
Copy codeCREATE STREAM ... ON DYNAMIC TABLE <name>

APPEND_ONLY is not supported for streams on dynamic tables. If you need
insert-only semantics, consume the standard stream and filter on METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' in
your downstream task. Alternatively, custom incremental dynamic tables
support append-only semantics natively through the CHANGES(INFORMATION => APPEND_ONLY) clause.
NoteThe dynamic table must use an incremental refresh. Dynamic tables that use a full refresh don’t
support streams because each refresh replaces the entire table output, so there is no incremental
change history to track. If REFRESH_MODE is set to AUTO, verify the resolved mode by running
SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES and checking the refresh_mode column before creating a stream.

When to use this pattern
The primary use case is a hybrid pipeline where a dynamic table handles the declarative definition
and a triggered task handles imperative work the dynamic table can’t express:
Dynamic table -> stream -> triggered task -> target
Common scenarios:

Writing to a non-dynamic-table target (regular table, external stage).
Calling a stored procedure or external function with side effects.
Running conditional logic (IF/ELSE, loops) on the change set.

Use SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA in the task’s WHEN clause so the task fires only when the stream has
unconsumed changes. The task runs after the dynamic table refreshes and produces new output. A
refresh that changes no rows doesn’t trigger the task.
Copy code-- Create a triggered task that consumes the stream
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK load_completed_orders
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('dt_orders_stream')
AS
  INSERT INTO completed_orders_archive
  SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, product_name, line_total
  FROM dt_orders_stream
  WHERE order_status = 'completed';

If multiple tasks consume the same dynamic table, create a separate stream for each. See Introduction to streams for details.

Stream behavior after reinitialization
When a dynamic table reinitializes (for example,
after a CREATE OR REPLACE on a base table, a masking policy change, or a change-tracking toggle),
the stream survives but its next read can return a much larger set of change rows than a normal
refresh produces. The stream remains attached and exposes all row-level differences between its last-read offset and the reinitialized output.
WarningAfter reinitialization, rows that were previously updates will appear as DELETE + INSERT pairs with
METADATA$ISUPDATE set to FALSE. Downstream logic that relies on METADATA$ISUPDATE to distinguish
real deletes from updates can lose or duplicate data without an error. Use idempotent MERGE statements
rather than conditional INSERT/DELETE branching to handle this safely.
The following MERGE handles both normal changes and the DELETE + INSERT pairs that appear after
reinitialization. The three clauses cover deletes, updates, and inserts by matching on the primary
key:
Copy codeMERGE INTO completed_orders_archive t
USING (
    SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, product_name, line_total,
           METADATA$ACTION,
           METADATA$ISUPDATE
    FROM dt_orders_stream
    WHERE order_status = 'completed'
) s ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED
    AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'DELETE'
    AND NOT s.METADATA$ISUPDATE THEN
    DELETE
WHEN MATCHED
    AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN
    UPDATE SET t.customer_id  = s.customer_id,
               t.order_date   = s.order_date,
               t.product_name = s.product_name,
               t.line_total   = s.line_total
WHEN NOT MATCHED
    AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN
    INSERT (order_id, customer_id, order_date, product_name, line_total)
    VALUES (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.order_date, s.product_name, s.line_total);

After reinitialization, every surviving row appears as a DELETE + INSERT pair with
METADATA$ISUPDATE = FALSE. The MERGE processes each pair correctly: Clause 1 removes the old row,
Clause 3 re-inserts it. The net effect is the same data, with no duplicates or data loss. For normal
changes, Clause 2 handles updates in place.
Design your downstream task to handle these large change sets gracefully. Use idempotent inserts or
batch processing so that a post-reinitialization read doesn’t cause duplicate or missing data.

Limitation: streams capture net changes, not full history
Don’t use a stream on a dynamic table as an audit log. If a row is inserted and then updated within a single
refresh cycle, the stream shows only the final state. If the stream is not read between two
refreshes, the changes from both refreshes collapse into a single net result.
If you need every state transition for compliance or auditing, write directly to an append-only
table from your ingestion layer instead. See Introduction to streams for
more on how streams track changes.
Verify the stream
After creating the stream, confirm it is attached and not stale:
Copy codeSHOW STREAMS LIKE 'dt_orders_stream';

| name               | database_name | schema_name   | source_type  | mode  | stale |
|--------------------+---------------+---------------+--------------+-------+-------|
| DT_ORDERS_STREAM  | MY_DB         | PUBLIC        | Dynamic Table| DEFAULT| false |

active. If stale shows true, the stream has fallen behind the dynamic table’s change history
and must be recreated. To prevent staleness, make sure the stream is read regularly within the data
retention period. See Introduction to streams for details on stream
staleness.

Common error

NoteBy default, requests to the Cortex Agent REST API time out after 15 minutes. To run longer requests, set the background field to true in the request body. Background runs time out after 6 hours, and you can reconnect to them with the Stream Agent Run endpoint. Background runs are generally available on AWS and Azure, and they’re only available when you use threads to manage conversation history.
There are two methods to interact with an Agent:

Build an agent object and reference this agent object in a request to the agent:run API.

Use Cortex Agents and MCP servers in an app
This topic describes how a Snowflake Native App can create Cortex Agents
and Snowflake-managed MCP servers,
and how a provider can register an SPCS service endpoint as an SPCS-hosted MCP
server. With these capabilities, an app can offer a conversational experience
over its shared data and functionality, and expose its tools to other agents
inside or outside Snowflake.
Overview
A Snowflake Native App can include three kinds of AI objects:
Cortex AgentsAgents that the app creates in its setup script or at runtime. App-created
agents appear in Snowflake CoWork and are callable from the REST,
Python, and SQL APIs, just like standalone agents.Snowflake-managed MCP serversMCP servers that wrap Snowflake-native objects (Cortex Search services, Cortex
Analyst semantic views, Cortex Agents, UDFs, and stored procedures) as MCP
tools. The app creates these by using
CREATE MCP SERVER.SPCS-hosted MCP serversMCP servers that register an SPCS service endpoint with the MCP client
infrastructure used by Cortex Agents and Snowflake CoWork. They let
the app expose arbitrary code (in any language or framework) running in
Snowpark Container Services as MCP tools. The app creates these by using
CREATE CUSTOM MCP SERVER.
These capabilities are separate from, and complementary to, sharing agents
created in the provider account. For information about sharing standalone
agents, see Share Cortex Agents.
Security model
Cortex Agents created by an app run under
restricted caller’s rights (RCR). RCR enforces
that an app’s agent can’t access consumer data without an explicit grant from
the consumer.
Every tool invocation from an app-created agent requires both of the following:

Consumer privilege: a user in the consumer account has the privilege
needed on the target object. This is the same caller’s-rights model used by
standalone agents.
App caller grant: the consumer admin has performed a caller grant to
the app for the object. For more information, see
GRANT CALLER.

Key points:

The app gets implicit caller grants on objects that it owns. The provider
doesn’t need to request explicit caller grants for in-app objects.
Consumer-owned objects require explicit GRANT CALLER ... TO APPLICATION
from the consumer admin.
When a tool runs in owner’s rights (for example, a procedure created with
EXECUTE AS OWNER), execution switches to the owner’s identity. RCR
restrictions don’t apply within that tool’s scope.
When a tool runs in restricted caller’s rights, for example a procedure
created with EXECUTE AS RESTRICTED CALLER and owned by a role other
than the app, RCR restrictions compose by intersection. Each link in a
chain makes the effective access stricter, never looser.
Owner’s rights agents aren’t supported. A provider can still surface an agent
through an owner’s-rights code entity (for example, a Streamlit app or an
Snowpark Container Services service) that calls the agent using the app’s identity.

Snowflake-managed MCP servers created by an app are restricted to app-owned
tools. They can’t expose tools that aren’t owned by the app, and they can’t
include the SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL tool. This restriction prevents an installed
app’s MCP server from being used as a way to access consumer data or run
arbitrary SQL in the consumer’s account.
Before you begin
To use Cortex Agents in a Snowflake Native App, the consumer account must have both
Cortex Agents and Snowflake CoWork enabled. For more information, see
Cortex Agents.

Cortex Agents in a Native App
This section describes the provider and consumer admin workflows for creating
and using a Cortex Agent in a Snowflake Native App.
Provider: Create the agent
A provider creates an agent in the app’s setup script, or at runtime in a
code entity. The following example creates an agent that includes a Cortex
Analyst tool backed by an app-owned semantic view, a second Cortex Analyst tool
backed by a consumer-owned semantic view, and a custom procedure tool that calls
an app-owned procedure:
Copy codeCREATE OR REPLACE AGENT core.my_agent
  FROM SPECIFICATION $$
models:
  orchestration: auto
instructions:
  response: "Provide concise, accurate financial analysis answers."
  orchestration: "Use the Cortex Analyst tools for financial data questions."
tools:
  - tool_spec:
      type: "cortex_analyst_text_to_sql"
      name: "Analyst1"
      description: "Answers questions about the app's financial data"
  - tool_spec:
      type: "cortex_analyst_text_to_sql"
      name: "Analyst2"
      description: "Answers questions about the consumer's portfolio data"
  - tool_spec:
      type: generic
      name: Procedure1
      description: "Return current app metadata about the specified category"
      input_schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          category:
            type: string
            description: "Category of metadata to return"
        required: ["category"]
tool_resources:
  Analyst1:
    semantic_view: "core.my_semantic_view"
    execution_environment:
      type: warehouse
      warehouse: "MY_APP_WH"
  Analyst2:
    semantic_view: "consumer_db.public.consumer_semantic_view"
    execution_environment:
      type: warehouse
      warehouse: "MY_APP_WH"
  Procedure1:
    identifier: core.get_app_metadata
    type: procedure
    execution_environment:
      type: warehouse
      warehouse: "MY_APP_WH"
$$;

Notes:

Partially qualified identifiers (such as core.my_semantic_view) are
resolved relative to the agent’s database and schema. This is the
recommended pattern inside a Snowflake Native App, because the app database name is
only known at install time.
Tool identifiers aren’t resolved when the agent is created. A provider can
declare tools before the underlying objects are created or before the app
has access to them.
We recommend using orchestration: auto instead of a specific model name.
A specific model might not be available in the consumer’s region.

For information about Cortex Agent SQL commands, see
Cortex Agent commands.

Provider: Ship skills with the app
You can ship agent skills
with a Snowflake Native App by writing SKILL.md files to an app-owned internal stage
in the setup script, then referencing that stage from the agent specification.
Because the setup script runs in the consumer account, you can’t use PUT to
upload files from a local machine. Create an internal stage, unload the skill
content with COPY INTO <location>, and grant READ on
the stage to the application roles that should use the agent.
Each SKILL.md file uses YAML frontmatter for name and description. Put
the skill’s execution instructions in the Markdown body after the closing
---. Cortex Agents ignore an instructions key in the frontmatter.
The file format options in the following example write the skill content as
plain, uncompressed text. TYPE = CSV is the text-based unload format, and
setting COMPRESSION, RECORD_DELIMITER, and FIELD_DELIMITER to NONE
prevents Snowflake from compressing the output or inserting CSV delimiters into
the Markdown. SINGLE = TRUE writes one file instead of multiple files, and
the SKILL.md filename in the target path gives that file its name.
Copy codeCREATE STAGE IF NOT EXISTS core.skills_stage;

COPY INTO @core.skills_stage/app_skill/SKILL.md
  FROM (
    SELECT $$---
name: app_skill
description: Answers questions that match this skill's description.
---
Follow the app-specific workflow in this skill.
$$
  )
  FILE_FORMAT = (
    TYPE = CSV
    COMPRESSION = NONE
    RECORD_DELIMITER = NONE
    FIELD_DELIMITER = NONE
  )
  OVERWRITE = TRUE
  SINGLE = TRUE;

GRANT READ ON STAGE core.skills_stage TO APPLICATION ROLE my_app_role;

Then reference the skill folder (not the SKILL.md file) in the agent
specification. Use a partially qualified stage path so the path doesn’t depend
on the installed application database name:
Copy codeCREATE OR REPLACE AGENT core.my_agent
  FROM SPECIFICATION $$
models:
  orchestration: auto
instructions:
  response: "Provide concise answers. Use the app_skill when the question matches its description."
skills:
  - name: app_skill
    source:
      type: STAGE
      path: @core.skills_stage/app_skill
$$;

Repeat the COPY INTO statement for each skill, using a distinct folder under
the stage (for example @core.skills_stage/another_skill/SKILL.md). If a skill
includes supporting files, unload each file into the same folder with a
separate COPY INTO statement.
For general skill authoring and stage layout, see
Agent skills.
Provider: Create the tools and grant access
The application also creates the tools that the agent uses and grants access
to them through application roles:
Copy codeCREATE SEMANTIC VIEW core.my_semantic_view ...;
CREATE PROCEDURE core.get_app_metadata(category STRING) RETURNS STRING ...;

GRANT USAGE ON AGENT core.my_agent TO APPLICATION ROLE my_app_role;

GRANT SELECT ON SEMANTIC VIEW core.my_semantic_view
  TO APPLICATION ROLE my_app_role;
GRANT USAGE ON PROCEDURE core.get_app_metadata(STRING)
  TO APPLICATION ROLE my_app_role;

Consumer admin: Audit the agent before granting access
Before granting users access to an app-created agent, the consumer admin should
review the agent’s full specification (model, tools, system prompt, and
referenced objects) by using DESCRIBE AGENT or through
the agent UI:
Copy codeDESC AGENT my_app.core.my_agent;

Consumer admin: Grant caller access on consumer objects
Without caller grants, the agent can’t use consumer objects, even if the
consumer user has privileges on them. The following example grants the app the
caller privileges that the agent needs:

GRANT CALLER USAGE ON DATABASE my_db TO APPLICATION my_app;
GRANT CALLER USAGE ON SCHEMA my_db.my_schema TO APPLICATION my_app;

GRANT INHERITED CALLER SELECT ON ALL SEMANTIC VIEWS IN SCHEMA my_db.my_schema
  TO APPLICATION my_app;
GRANT INHERITED CALLER SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA my_db.my_schema

# Learning Path — Data Pipelines + AI Agents (Beginner → Winning Hackathon Build)

**Target:** Banking/NBFC risk & compliance copilot (see `REQUIREMENTS.md`).
**Philosophy:** Do not learn theory then build. Build the actual solution in thin vertical slices, learning each concept at the moment you need it. Every stage below produces a working artifact you can demo.

---

## 0. The Mental Model (read this first — 10 minutes)

Your solution is four layers. Learn them in this order, bottom-up.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  4. SURFACE     Streamlit app / CoCo CLI / Slack            │  ← what judges see
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  3. AGENT       Cortex Agent = LLM + tools + instructions   │  ← the "copilot"
│                 tools: Analyst (SQL), Search (docs), custom │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  2. SEMANTIC    Semantic view (structured) +                │  ← makes NL → data safe
│                 Cortex Search service (unstructured)        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  1. PIPELINE    Raw → dynamic tables → risk signals        │  ← the data foundation
│                 + streams/tasks for actions & audit         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**The single most important idea:** an AI agent is only as good as layer 2. Beginners spend all their time on prompts and lose. Winners spend their time making the semantic layer so clean that the agent almost cannot get it wrong.

**Why an agent needs a semantic view at all:** an LLM writing raw SQL against 40 tables guesses at joins and grain, and silently returns wrong numbers. A semantic view declares the entities, metrics, and relationships once, so the agent picks from a governed menu instead of inventing SQL. That is what "governed and explainable" means in practice.

---

## Stage 1 — Foundations: make data appear (Day 1)

### Concepts to learn
| Concept | What it is | Why you need it |
|---|---|---|
| Warehouse | Compute. Costs credits when running. | Every pipeline needs one. |
| Database / Schema | Namespace: `DB.SCHEMA.OBJECT` | Everything is addressed this way. |
| Table vs View | Stored rows vs saved query | View = no storage, recomputed each time. |
| Medallion layering | `RAW` → `CLEAN` → `MART` | Non-negotiable for a judged build. Shows you think in layers. |

### Build
Set up three schemas: `RAW`, `CURATED`, `RISK`. Plus `GOVERNANCE` for audit/evidence.

Generate synthetic data via CoCo (**this is requirement RT-1 — do not skip, and do not use real data**). You need referential consistency: every transaction's `account_id` must exist in accounts; every account's `customer_id` must exist in customers.

Minimum viable banking dataset:
- `customers` — id, name, country, risk_rating, pep_flag, onboarding_date
- `accounts` — id, customer_id, product_type, open_date, balance, currency
- `transactions` — id, account_id, ts, amount, currency, channel, counterparty_id, counterparty_country, mcc
- `counterparties` — id, name, country, sanctions_flag
- `loans` — id, customer_id, principal, rate, term, dpd (days past due), collateral_value
- `policy_documents` — the unstructured half: AML policy, sanctions policy, KYC procedure, Basel LCR methodology, internal thresholds doc

**Deliberately plant the fraud patterns you intend to detect.** If you generate purely random data, your agent will find nothing and your demo dies. Plant:
- **Structuring/smurfing** — many deposits just under a reporting threshold (e.g. 9 × ₹49,000 when the threshold is ₹50,000)
- **Round-tripping** — A→B→C→A within a short window
- **Dormant-then-active** — account idle 18 months, then sudden high-value outflow
- **High-risk-corridor** — transfers to a sanctioned or high-risk jurisdiction
- **Velocity spike** — 30× normal daily transaction count
- **Credit deterioration** — a cohort whose DPD walks 0 → 30 → 60 → 90

Keep a hidden ground-truth table (`GOVERNANCE.planted_cases`) listing exactly which entities carry which pattern. This becomes your test oracle in Stage 7 — it is the difference between claiming accuracy and proving it.

### How to learn this with CoCo
Ask CoCo to design the schema and generate the data, but **read what it produces and ask it why**. Prompt it for the reasoning: "why did you make counterparty_country separate from counterparty?" You learn faster interrogating a design than reading docs.

---

## Stage 2 — Pipelines: the core skill (Days 2–3)

This is the part you said you most need. Learn it in this exact order.

### 2a. Understand the three pipeline tools

| Tool | Model | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **Dynamic table** | Declarative — you write a `SELECT`, Snowflake keeps it fresh | Default choice for SQL transformations with joins/aggregations |
| **Stream + Task** | Procedural — stream captures changes, task runs code | You need `MERGE`, stored procedures, external calls, sub-minute, or SCD2 |
| **Materialized view** | Single-table query acceleration, always current | Read performance on one table, not a pipeline |

**Dynamic table, minimal form:**
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE risk.dt_txn_enriched
  TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL
AS
  SELECT t.txn_id, t.account_id, a.customer_id, t.ts, t.amount,
         c.country AS cp_country, c.sanctions_flag
  FROM raw.transactions t
  JOIN raw.accounts a       ON a.account_id = t.account_id
  LEFT JOIN raw.counterparties c ON c.counterparty_id = t.counterparty_id;
```

Read it as three decisions:
1. **`TARGET_LAG`** — a *freshness goal*, not a schedule. "Never more than 5 minutes stale." Snowflake decides when to actually refresh, and skips refreshes entirely when base tables have not changed. Minimum is 1 minute.
2. **`REFRESH_MODE`** — `INCREMENTAL` reprocesses only changed rows (fast, cheap). `FULL` rebuilds everything. `AUTO` lets Snowflake pick — and will silently fall back to `FULL` if your SQL is not incrementalizable. **Always set `INCREMENTAL` explicitly** so you get a hard error instead of a silent cost blowup.
3. **The `SELECT`** — that is the entire transformation. No `INSERT`, no `MERGE`, no procedural code.

### 2b. Chain them into a pipeline

Intermediate tables use `TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM` — they refresh only as needed to satisfy the final table's goal. Only the terminal table carries a real freshness number. Snowflake works out dependency order automatically.

```
raw.transactions
      ↓
dt_txn_enriched          TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM
      ↓
dt_txn_features          TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM   (rolling windows, velocity, z-scores)
      ↓
dt_fraud_signals         TARGET_LAG = '5 minutes'  ← terminal, drives the whole chain
```

Build the same 3-level chain for credit risk (`dpd` buckets → PD proxy → portfolio expected loss) and liquidity (inflow/outflow by bucket → LCR-style ratio).

### 2c. Learn the limits before they bite you

Commit these to memory — each one is a build-breaker you will otherwise hit at 2am:

- **No DML on a dynamic table.** They are read-only. No `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`/`TRUNCATE`.
- **No `MERGE`** in a standard dynamic table definition. Express "latest state per key" as `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY ts DESC) = 1` instead.
- **No stored procedures, external functions, or side effects** in the definition. It is a pure `SELECT`.
- **No `RANDOM()`, `UUID_STRING()`, or sequence functions** in incremental mode — the `CREATE` fails outright if you set `REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL`. Generate surrogate keys upstream or use deterministic hashes.
- **No SCD Type 2 history.** A dynamic table represents *current state*. Point-in-time history needs streams + tasks or an append-only table.
- **Cannot read from** external tables, directory tables, streams, or materialized views.
- **Changing the definition triggers reinitialization** — the whole table reprocesses.
- **1 minute is the floor** for `TARGET_LAG`. "Real-time" in your PS means near-real-time; say so honestly rather than overclaiming.

### 2d. The hybrid pattern — where the imperative half lives

Your PS needs *actions*: create a case record, write an audit entry, fire a notification. Dynamic tables cannot do side effects. The bridge is a stream on the dynamic table feeding a triggered task:

```
dt_fraud_signals → stream → triggered task → case table / notification
```

```sql
-- NOTE: ON DYNAMIC TABLE, not ON TABLE. ON TABLE errors out.
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM risk.fraud_signals_stream
  ON DYNAMIC TABLE risk.dt_fraud_signals;

CREATE OR REPLACE TASK risk.open_fraud_cases
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('risk.fraud_signals_stream')
AS
  INSERT INTO governance.fraud_cases (case_id, entity_id, signal_type, score, detected_at)
  SELECT ...
  FROM risk.fraud_signals_stream
  WHERE METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' AND score >= 80;
```

Three gotchas that matter here:
- The upstream dynamic table **must** use incremental refresh — full-refresh tables cannot have streams, because each refresh replaces the entire output.
- **Only `standard` (delta) streams** work on dynamic tables. `APPEND_ONLY` is not supported; filter on `METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT'` downstream instead.
- **Use an idempotent `MERGE`, not conditional INSERT/DELETE branching.** After a reinitialization, every surviving row reappears as a `DELETE` + `INSERT` pair with `METADATA$ISUPDATE = FALSE`. Logic that trusts `METADATA$ISUPDATE` to distinguish real deletes from updates will duplicate or lose data *with no error raised*.

### 2e. The audit-trail decision (your PS lives or dies here)

**A stream is not an audit log.** It returns net changes since last read. Insert-then-update between two reads collapses to one row. If nobody reads the stream between two refreshes, both refreshes collapse into a single net result.

"Audit-ready" means every state transition is preserved. So:

> Write evidence **append-only from the ingestion layer**, never reconstruct it from a stream.

Design `GOVERNANCE.evidence_log` as insert-only: `(evidence_id, case_id, captured_at, source_object, source_row_key, snapshot VARIANT, policy_ref, captured_by)`. Every signal the pipeline raises inserts a frozen snapshot of the evidence *at detection time*. When a regulator asks "what did you know on 14 March", you can answer. This single design choice is what separates a real compliance build from a dashboard.

### 2f. Learn to operate, not just create
- `SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES` — check the `refresh_mode` column to see what `AUTO` actually resolved to.
- `SHOW STREAMS` — check the `stale` column. A stale stream has fallen outside the retention window and must be recreated. Read streams regularly.
- Ask CoCo to run a refresh-health check and explain any failure. Learning to read `DYNAMIC_TABLE_REFRESH_HISTORY` is a genuine skill and demonstrates operational maturity to judges.

---

## Stage 3 — Unstructured: policy and filing text (Day 4)

Requirement FR-1 demands both halves. Structured-only is an automatic loss.

### Concepts
- **Parsing** — `AI_PARSE_DOCUMENT` turns a PDF on a stage into text/OCR output.
- **Extraction** — `AI_EXTRACT` pulls named fields (threshold values, effective dates, jurisdictions) into columns.
- **Chunking** — split long documents into passages; retrieval works on passages, not whole files.
- **Cortex Search service** — managed semantic + keyword retrieval over a text column. This is what makes a document citable.
- **Classification** — `AI_CLASSIFY` to route documents by type (AML / Basel / KYC / local).

### Build
1. Stage your synthetic policy PDFs.
2. Parse → chunk → a `policy_chunks` table with `(chunk_text, doc_name, section, page, effective_date, jurisdiction)`.
3. Create a Cortex Search service over `chunk_text`, with the metadata columns as attributes so the agent can filter by jurisdiction or date.
4. Extract the hard numbers — reporting thresholds, LCR minimums, holding periods — into a structured `policy_thresholds` table.

**The step almost everyone misses:** join `policy_thresholds` back into your pipeline so detection rules *read their thresholds from the policy table*. Then when the agent says "this breached the ₹50,000 structuring threshold", it can cite the document, page, and effective date that set that number. That is evidence-backed rather than hardcoded — and it is the most persuasive thirty seconds of your demo.

Keep the metadata (`doc_name`, `section`, `page`, `effective_date`) on every chunk. Without it you can retrieve text but cannot cite it, and an uncitable answer is not audit-ready.

---

## Stage 4 — Semantic layer: where the agent gets its intelligence (Day 5)

### Concepts
- **Semantic view** — declares logical tables, relationships, dimensions, metrics, and synonyms over your physical tables. Cortex Analyst uses it to turn NL into SQL.
- **Verified queries (VQRs)** — human-approved question→SQL pairs. The highest-leverage accuracy tool you have.
- **Ontology** — your domain vocabulary: what *is* a customer, an exposure, a case, a breach, and how they relate.

### Build
Author a semantic view over the `RISK` marts (not raw tables). Define, with synonyms:
- Entities: customer, account, transaction, counterparty, loan, case
- Metrics: exposure, expected loss, NPA ratio, LCR, transaction velocity, fraud score
- Dimensions: jurisdiction, product, risk rating, DPD bucket, time grain

Add verified queries for every question you plan to demo, plus the ten most likely judge questions. Then **validate the view against natural-language questions** — that is explicitly requirement RT-3, and CoCo can generate a question set and check the SQL it produces.

**Beginner traps:**
- Metric grain. "Total exposure" summed over a joined transaction table double-counts via fan-out. Define metrics at their correct grain and test one against a hand-written SQL number.
- Synonyms. Compliance users say "NPA", "bad loan", "stressed asset", "DPD 90+" for the same thing. If synonyms are missing the agent fails on phrasing, not on data.
- Never point the semantic view at raw tables. Point it at curated marts so business logic lives in one place.

---

## Stage 5 — The agent (Day 6)

### Concepts

A Cortex Agent is an **agent object** holding: models + instructions + tools + tool_resources. It reasons, plans, calls tools, and iterates — you do not write the orchestration loop.

Tool types you will use:
| Tool type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `cortex_analyst_text_to_sql` | NL → SQL over a semantic view (the structured half) |
| `cortex_search` | Retrieval over policy/filing text (the unstructured half) |
| `generic` | A custom function/procedure the agent can call to **take an action** |

`tool_resources` binds each tool to a concrete object — `semantic_view` for Analyst, `search_service` for Search, `identifier` + `execution_environment` for a function.

Two distinct instruction slots, and confusing them is a common beginner error:
- `instructions.response` — how to *speak* (tone, format, citation requirements)
- `instructions.orchestration` — how to *choose tools* ("for exposure or portfolio numbers use Analyst; for any policy, threshold, or regulation question use Search; always cite the policy section")

Set `models.orchestration: auto` rather than pinning a model name — a pinned model may not exist in the judging region. Set `orchestration.budget` (`seconds`, `tokens`) so runs terminate predictably in a live demo.

### Build
1. Agent with two tools: Analyst (semantic view) + Search (policy service). Test it. This alone satisfies FR-1 and FR-2.
2. Add `generic` tools that take real action (bonus B-4): `open_case`, `attach_evidence`, `generate_str_draft`, `escalate_to_reviewer`. These are stored procedures that write to `GOVERNANCE` tables. This converts read-only analysis into the signal→evidence→finding flow of FR-3.
3. Add **agent skills** — `SKILL.md` files on a stage, referenced from the agent spec, encoding your procedures: "how to investigate a structuring alert", "how to assemble an STR". YAML frontmatter carries `name` and `description`; the instructions go in the Markdown body. Skills are the headline bonus (B-1) — write them cleanly enough that another team could reuse them.
4. Run it three ways to prove cross-surface capability (B-6): the `agent:run` REST API, the `DATA_AGENT_RUN` SQL function, and Snowsight/CoWork.

### Guardrails (B-7 — cheap to add, disproportionately impressive)
- Confidence thresholds: below a bar, the agent says "insufficient evidence" rather than guessing. A compliance copilot that fabricates is worse than none, and judges in this domain know it.
- Every numeric claim carries the object it came from; every policy claim carries doc + section.
- `orchestration.tool_not_accessible` defaults to `accept` — the run continues with whatever tools the caller's role can reach and reports the rest as warnings. Decide deliberately whether that is the behaviour you want, and mention the choice in your demo.
- Governance is real, not decorative: masking policies on PII, row access policies by role, so the copilot is genuinely governed rather than merely described as governed.

---

## Stage 6 — Surface + orchestration (Day 7)

- **Streamlit app** (RT-4), scaffolded via CoCo. Four panes map exactly onto the judged flow: *Signals* → *Investigate* (agent chat) → *Evidence* → *Report*. Include action buttons so users act inside the solution, not just read it.
- **Automation** (B-3): schedule the pipeline refresh, a nightly signal sweep, and a scheduled regulatory-report draft via CoCo automations. Unattended operation is explicitly called for in the Execution phase.
- **MCP** (RT-5 / B-2): wire in Jira (create an investigation ticket) or Slack (alert the compliance channel). `CREATE MCP SERVER` wraps your own Snowflake objects — search services, semantic views, agents, UDFs, procedures — as MCP tools for other agents to consume. That is a strong ingenuity story in both directions.
- **Multi-agent** (B-5): a Detection agent, an Investigation agent, and a Reporting agent with explicit handoffs beats one monolithic agent, and reads as deliberate architecture.

---

## Stage 7 — Test and prove it (Day 8 — do not compress this)

This stage is where most hackathon teams lose points, because they demo happy paths only.

1. **Accuracy against ground truth.** Use `GOVERNANCE.planted_cases`. Report precision and recall per fraud pattern. Actual numbers beat adjectives every time.
2. **NL robustness.** Ask each demo question five ways, including with domain jargon and typos. Fix the semantic view's synonyms, not the prompt.
3. **Agent evaluations.** Use Snowsight Evaluations / `EXECUTE_AI_EVALUATION` to batch-test and baseline. Being able to say "we evaluated 60 questions and scored X on SQL correctness" is Technical Execution evidence in one sentence.
4. **Edge cases.** Empty result sets, a question outside scope, a question the data cannot answer, a policy that has no matching document, a NULL-heavy account, a currency mismatch. The correct behaviour is a graceful, honest refusal.
5. **Pipeline failure drills.** Suspend the warehouse mid-refresh; break a base table; let a stream go stale. Show recovery.
6. **Governance test.** Log in as a restricted role and prove the copilot returns less. Governance you can *demonstrate* is worth ten times governance you assert.

---

## What actually wins (ranked by return on effort)

1. **The signal→evidence→report loop closing end-to-end, live.** Most teams demo a chatbot answering questions. Show a fraud signal firing, evidence auto-assembled with citations, an STR draft generated, and a Jira ticket opened. That is the PS, satisfied literally.
2. **Citations on every claim.** Numbers cite the object; policy statements cite doc + section + effective date. This is the cheapest credibility you can buy.
3. **Thresholds read from policy text, not hardcoded.** Directly demonstrates FR-1 fusion in a way judges immediately understand.
4. **The append-only evidence log.** Says "we understand what audit-ready means" better than any slide.
5. **A clean, documented, reusable skill.** Explicitly the headline bonus.
6. **Measured accuracy against planted ground truth.** Turns Technical Execution from a claim into a number.
7. **Visible CoCo usage in all four phases.** Keep session transcripts, plans, and generated artifacts. Judges look for evidence at every stage — capture it as you go, because reconstructing it afterwards is painful and obvious.

## What loses

- A chatbot over one table with no pipeline and no documents.
- Real or scraped production-like data (privacy failure; synthetic is explicitly required).
- An agent that hallucinates a plausible number with no provenance.
- Random synthetic data with no planted patterns — nothing to detect, so nothing to demo.
- Governance mentioned in narration but never demonstrated.
- No CoCo evidence for the planning or testing phases.
- Overclaiming "real-time" when `TARGET_LAG` floors at 1 minute. Say near-real-time and be precise about the number.

---

## Day-by-day

| Day | Focus | Artifact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Setup, ontology, synthetic data + planted patterns | Populated `RAW` + ground-truth table |
| 2 | Dynamic tables, 3-level fraud chain | `dt_fraud_signals` refreshing |
| 3 | Credit + liquidity chains; streams/tasks; evidence log | Full pipeline + append-only audit |
| 4 | Documents: parse, chunk, Search service, thresholds | Citable policy corpus |
| 5 | Semantic view, metrics, synonyms, verified queries | Validated semantic layer |
| 6 | Agent: tools, instructions, skills, custom actions | Working copilot |
| 7 | Streamlit, automations, MCP, multi-agent | Demoable end-to-end system |
| 8 | Accuracy, evaluations, edge cases, governance, rehearsal | Test report + demo script |

If time runs short, cut Stage 6's MCP and multi-agent work — they are bonuses. **Never cut Stage 7.** A narrower solution that is proven correct scores higher on Solution Completeness than a broad one that visibly breaks on stage.

---

## How to use CoCo to learn (not just to generate)

- **Ask for the reasoning, then the code.** "Explain the tradeoff, then implement it" teaches you; "write this" does not.
- **Have it critique its own output.** "What breaks in this pipeline at 100× volume? What is not incrementalizable here?"
- **Make it quiz you.** "Give me five questions about dynamic table refresh modes, then grade my answers."
- **Never paste SQL you cannot read.** If you cannot explain a line, ask before you run it. Judges ask "why did you do it this way", and that is where borrowed code shows.
- **Keep the transcripts.** They are simultaneously your notes and your CoCo-usage evidence.
